items.why: The final sentence explicitly contrasts the five men entering with the priest and armed men remaining at the gate.
The sequence clearly distinguishes the five men’s initial removal from the priest’s later taking of the items.
“Our king” clearly refers to the trees, while gods and humans occur only in the vine’s reply.
A direct causal statement links their prosperity to the land lacking nothing.
The passage explicitly gives their lack of an inheritance as the reason for seeking land.
Jotham’s fear of Abimelek is explicit, although “lives elsewhere” is slightly imprecise.
The passage clearly separates the relatives receiving Abimelek’s instruction from the citizens who are its audience.
The Levite’s purpose in leaving is stated directly, while Micah’s house is only where he subsequently arrives.
The key is a conditional wish rather than a clear request, making the temporal wording awkward.
“Does something” is too vague to test meaningful comprehension, and the competitor is implausible.
The reported departure into the fields directly motivates the ambush, unlike the later observed movement from the city.
The mother’s wording assigns the making to her son, though the later silversmith creates some interpretive friction.
The servant unambiguously kills Abimelek, though the competing answer is very weak.
The occupants’ deaths are directly attributed to the stronghold being set on fire.
The passage clearly distinguishes the priestly service ending at captivity from the idol’s use during Shiloh’s period.
The shouting and overtaking occur together, so the precise cause of the Danites turning is not uniquely discriminating.
The fig tree’s rhetorical reply clearly identifies surrendering its sweet fruit as its reason for refusing.
Approaching the doorway is specifically tied to setting the tower on fire, while attacking is the broader action.
The object of “take it over” is clearly the land, though the generic reference to “listeners” is less natural.
Micah explicitly says God will favor him because the Levite has become his priest.
The route order supports the answer, but “the residence the Danites visit” is cumbersome and redundant.
The surrounding references to Jerub-Baal and “my father” resolve the pronoun, though it requires careful tracking.
Zebul is explicitly identified as secretly sending the messengers, sharply contrasting him with Gaal.
The men address the priest to inquire of God, clearly distinguishing the intermediary from the ultimate source.
The question treats Jotham’s curse as occurring after the punishment even though the text presents it as part of that punishment.
Zebul directly recasts the supposed people as mountain shadows in response to Gaal’s first claim.
The stated purpose clause directly links the citizens listening to God listening to them.
The olive tree explicitly frames giving up its honoring oil as the reason it will not rule.
Micah directly identifies his mother as the person who uttered the curse.
The passage explicitly says they cursed Abimelek while eating and drinking at the festival.
The passage directly gives both isolation from Sidon and lack of outside relationships as the reasons no one rescues them.
